items.answer: It fails for models whose preprocessing depends on image content or aspect ratio. The OCR composite has a different layout from the bare semantic image, so such a model may resize or crop the semantic content differently under OCR. Part of the carrier difference could then come from how the visual context was processed, not from where the instruction was placed.
rubric: Says the comparison can fail or be confounded for models whose preprocessing depends on image content or aspect ratio
Explains that the OCR composite has a different layout or aspect ratio than the TEXT image, so the semantic image may be resized or cropped differently, changing the visual context

items.question: In the full configuration's scenario-by-carrier cross-tabulation for one model, an auditor finds one cell with by far the highest ASR and reports it as the model's main weakness. Why might that conclusion not hold?
items.answer: The table has 18 scenarios × 2 carriers = 36 cells, each with relatively few responses. With that many cells, one cell can look extreme by chance. The paper warns against drawing conclusions from individual cells without accounting for multiple comparisons, and recommends aggregating to domain level when intervals are wide.
rubric: Says the single extreme cell may be a chance finding rather than a real weakness
Explains this by the many cells (about 36) each with few responses, so multiple comparisons or wide intervals must be accounted for, or results aggregated to domain level

items.question: A user applies the representation tooling to Code-framed versus Story-framed matched pairs and finds a large layer-wise divergence. Why might this not show anything about safety processing?
items.answer: The two templates differ greatly in surface form and in the kind of output they request. The final generation-prefix state may therefore separate them because it encodes format or genre rather than anything safety-related. The tooling is only correlational, so intervention would be needed to link the divergence to refusal behaviour.
rubric: Says the divergence may not reflect safety processing
Explains that Code and Story templates differ strongly in surface form or requested output format, which the prefix representation could encode
Notes that the analysis is correlational, so intervention would be needed to support a safety interpretation

items.question: Under the OCR carrier, why might mismatch rates be higher for Identity Credential and Authorization Document instances than for Danger instances, for reasons unrelated to reading the rendered instruction?
items.answer: Images in those two categories were generated to contain coherent text. An OCR instance in these categories therefore shows two text sources, the rendered instruction and the document text. A model may transcribe or respond to the document text instead of the instruction, and the judge flags only transcribing visual content as a mismatch. Category differences in OCR mismatch can therefore reflect competing text rather than instruction legibility.
rubric: Says the extra mismatches can come from text inside the credential or document images, not from difficulty reading the instruction
Explains that a model may transcribe or answer the document text instead of the instruction, which the judge counts as a mismatch (e.g., only transcribing visual content)

items.question: The exported stratified tables give bootstrap confidence intervals computed by resampling intents. When would these intervals understate the real uncertainty of a stratum's ASR or CASR?
items.answer: They understate uncertainty when the judge errs systematically within that stratum. Resampling intents captures only variation over which intents were sampled. It does not capture judge error, such as GPT-5's imperfect mismatch detection (macro-F1 0.85). A bias concentrated in one framing, category or carrier would shift the estimate without widening its interval.
rubric: Says the intervals understate uncertainty when the judge makes systematic errors in that stratum
Explains that resampling intents captures only intent-sampling variability and not judge error (for example, mismatch macro-F1 of only 0.85)

items.question: An auditor reads the pooled harm-domain table across all 16 models and concludes that the domain with the highest pooled ASR is the riskiest domain for the specific model the company deploys. When would that inference fail?
items.answer: It fails when the deployed model's own profile differs from the pool. Pooled tables average over models, and the paper stresses that behaviour is model-dependent: it provides per-model tables and recommends reading carrier results per model. The auditor should read that model's own stratified table instead.
rubric: Says the inference fails when the deployed model's own domain profile differs from the pooled average
Explains that pooled tables average over 16 models whose behaviour is model-dependent, so the per-model stratified table should be used

items.question: Why does Table 11 report Lin's concordance correlation in addition to Spearman's ρ to argue that lightweight ASRs can stand in for full-configuration ASRs?
items.answer: Spearman's ρ measures only whether the cells are ranked in the same order. Lightweight ASRs that were all shifted or rescaled would still score near 1. Lin's CCC also penalizes departures from the identity line, so its value of 0.999 shows that the actual ASR values agree, not just their ordering.
rubric: States that Spearman captures only rank or order agreement, which a constant shift or rescaling would not affect
States that Lin's CCC measures agreement in absolute values (closeness to the identity line), so it supports using the lightweight numbers directly

items.question: Why can a model that fully goes along with the Academic template, engaging willingly with the request, still not be counted as jailbroken?
items.answer: The Academic template asks the model to analyse the topic and discuss related aspects. A compliant answer can therefore stay at a high-level, non-operational analysis. The rubric scores such answers 2 or 3, and ASR counts only scores of 4 or higher, meaning actionable harmful assistance.
rubric: States that following the Academic framing can yield high-level or partial, non-actionable discussion
States that such responses score 2–3 and fall below the s≥4 success threshold

items.question: Why is the paper's near-duplicate removal based on pairwise cosine similarity with manual review rather than on the PCA visualization of intent embeddings?
items.answer: Removing near-duplicates means finding specific pairs of intents that are too similar. A pairwise similarity distribution exposes those pairs as a high-similarity tail that can be inspected one by one. The PCA plot is a qualitative 2-D projection that only shows overall spread, and nearby points in it cannot reliably identify duplicate pairs.
rubric: States that duplicate detection requires identifying specific similar pairs, which the pairwise similarity tail provides for manual review
States that the PCA view is only a qualitative low-dimensional projection of overall coverage and cannot pinpoint duplicates

items.question: Why would a 10-point ASR increase confined to Violence & Physical Harm move a model's aggregate ASR almost three times as much as a 10-point increase confined to Sexual Content?
items.answer: Aggregate ASR pools all instances, and each intent is instantiated under the same framings, images and carriers. Each domain therefore weighs in proportion to its number of intents: 48 intents (17.6%) for Violence & Physical Harm versus 17 (6.3%) for Sexual Content. The increases would add about 1.8 versus 0.6 points to the aggregate, a ratio of about 2.8.
rubric: States that aggregate ASR weights domains by their share of instances (17.6% vs 6.3%, or 48 vs 17 intents)
Gives the resulting effect: about 1.76 vs 0.63 points, a ratio of roughly 2.8

items.question: In the per-model sensitivity profiles, why could a model's ASR range across framing templates exceed its range across carriers even if the model were equally sensitive to both dimensions?
items.answer: The range is the gap between the highest and lowest configuration. Framing has 6 configurations and carrier has only 2. With more levels, there are more chances for an extreme value, including through sampling noise, so the max-minus-min tends to be larger. Ranges across dimensions with different numbers of levels are not like-for-like.
rubric: States that the range is max minus min across configurations, so it grows with the number of configurations
Notes that framing has 6 configurations versus 2 for carrier, so the two ranges are not directly comparable

items.question: Why does comparing a semantic category such as Danger against the nature control test something different from comparing Danger against Role?
items.answer: Semantic images are generated per intent, as V(h,v) from intent-specific descriptions, so both Danger and Role images are tailored to the request. The nature control is generic and unrelated to any harmful intent. Danger versus nature therefore mixes intent relevance with category meaning, while Danger versus Role holds intent relevance fixed and varies only the kind of contextual signal.
rubric: States that semantic images are intent-specific (generated from the intent, V(h,v)) while the nature control is generic and unrelated to the intent
Concludes that semantic-vs-nature confounds intent relevance with category meaning, while category-vs-category isolates the type of contextual signal

items.question: Roughly how many lightweight-configuration instances would a single model see for Violence & Physical Harm under the OCR carrier?
items.answer: About 130. The lightweight configuration preserves the full-configuration distribution, giving Violence & Physical Harm about 17.6% of 1,500, roughly 264 instances, and each carrier about half of those.
rubric: Gives about 130 instances (acceptable range roughly 120–140)
Derives it from preserved proportions: about 17.6% of 1,500 for the domain, split about equally between the 2 carriers

items.question: A policy team cares specifically about suicide and self-harm requests. Which level of the harm-intent stratification should it read, and why?
items.answer: It should read the scenario level. Suicide & Self-Harm is one of three scenarios inside the Violence & Physical Harm domain, alongside Violence & Terrorism and Weapons & CBRN. The domain-level ASR averages over all three and could hide a high or low rate on self-harm. The scenario stratum has 15 intents.
rubric: Recommends the scenario-level stratification rather than the domain level
Explains that Suicide & Self-Harm is pooled with two other scenarios in the Violence & Physical Harm domain, so the domain rate could mask its behaviour

items.question: A company puts a filter in front of its MLLM that scans only the text part of each prompt for harmful requests. Which part of MMJailBench is most informative about whether this filter can be bypassed, and what should be reported?
items.answer: The OCR carrier is the most informative. It delivers the same instruction inside an image, so a text-only filter never sees it. The company should report OCR ASR together with the mismatch rate and CASR, so that low success caused by the model failing to read the image is not mistaken for filter effectiveness.
rubric: Identifies the OCR carrier as the relevant probe, because the instruction is embedded in the image and invisible to a text-only filter
Says to report OCR mismatch rate and CASR alongside ASR, to separate perception failures from real protection

items.question: A reviewer worries that GPT-5 judging gpt-5's own responses is biased and proposes re-scoring them with the paper's lightweight judge as an independent check. Is this a good check, and what would be better?
items.answer: No. The lightweight judge was trained on GPT-5 annotations and validated only for agreement with GPT-5, so it would reproduce any GPT-5 bias rather than reveal it. A better check is human-expert annotation of a sample of gpt-5's responses, or a different judge re-validated against humans on a sample.
rubric: Says the lightweight judge is not an independent check
Explains that it is distilled from and validated against GPT-5, so it inherits GPT-5's biases
Recommends human annotation of a sample or a separately validated judge instead

items.question: A team wants to run all four control image conditions alongside the five semantic categories in the full configuration. By roughly what factor would the number of evaluated instances grow?
items.answer: By about 1.8×. The visual dimension would go from 5 to 9 conditions while intents, framings and carriers stay fixed, since the controls are paired with the same instruction components.
rubric: Gives a growth factor of about 1.8 (9/5), or an 80% increase
Explains that only the visual dimension grows, from 5 to 9 conditions, with the other dimensions unchanged

items.question: A researcher wants to know whether the internal difference between Authorization Document and Danger contexts on gemma3-12b is shared by Identity Credential versus Danger contexts. How can the paper's tooling test this, and how far can the result be interpreted?
items.answer: Fit the difference direction on Authorization Document-versus-Danger discovery pairs. Then project held-out Identity Credential-versus-Danger matched pairs onto that fixed direction; the tooling allows any two visual conditions to be substituted. Consistent projection would show a shared representational difference. It would remain correlational and would need intervention to support causal claims.
rubric: Describes fitting the direction on Authorization Document vs Danger pairs and projecting Identity Credential vs Danger matched pairs onto it
States that a positive result is correlational, with intervention needed for causal conclusions

items.question: If all five visual categories had been generated with FLUX.2 instead of splitting between zimage and FLUX.2, which caveat on visual-semantics comparisons would be removed, and which would remain?
items.answer: The confound from using different image generators across categories would be removed. The caveat about textual legibility would remain: Identity Credential and Authorization Document images would still contain coherent text that the other categories lack, and this can interact with a model's perception. Category differences would still not be pure differences in meaning.
rubric: Says the generator difference between categories would no longer confound comparisons
Says the difference in textual content or legibility between text-bearing document categories and scene categories would still interact with perception

items.question: If every harm domain had contained exactly 30 intents, which of the paper's reporting recommendations would lose most of its stated motivation?
items.answer: The advice to report per-domain counts alongside rates, and the specific caution about wider confidence intervals for small domains such as Sexual Content, would lose most of their motivation. Both rest on domains differing in size: 48 intents for Violence & Physical Harm versus 17 for Sexual Content. Equal sizes would also give every domain equal weight in aggregate ASR.
rubric: Names the recommendation to report counts alongside rates and/or the caution about wide CIs for small domains like Sexual Content
Explains that these rest on unequal domain sizes (e.g., 48 vs 17 intents), which equal sizes would remove

items.question: If the judge had output only a binary jailbreak label instead of a 1–5 harmfulness score, which validation statistic and which user-facing feature described in the paper would no longer be possible?
items.answer: QWK could not be computed, because it measures agreement on an ordinal scale. Users also could not re-threshold the released score distribution, for example to also count partial-information responses. The paper's distinction between topical engagement (scores 2–3) and actionable assistance (4–5) would no longer be visible.
rubric: Names QWK as a validation statistic that would no longer be possible, because it requires ordinal scores
Names the released score distribution, or applying alternative thresholds, as a feature that would be lost

items.question: If the framing templates had been optimized adaptively for each model instead of being fixed, which property of the framing stratification would be lost?
items.answer: Framing ASRs would no longer be repeatable probes applied identically to every model and study. Cross-model and cross-study comparisons per template would therefore lose their basis, because each model would face different prompts. Adaptive templates might come closer to worst-case robustness, but that is not what the fixed design measures.
rubric: Says repeatability, or identical conditions across models and studies, would be lost
Explains that per-template comparisons across models or studies depend on every model receiving the same fixed prompts

items.question: Suppose the human-validation sample had contained almost no responses that experts scored 4 or 5, yet still showed QWK 0.97 and ΔASR +0.3%. Which claim would be weakly supported despite these numbers?
items.answer: The claim that GPT-5 reliably applies the s≥4 success threshold, and so the reported ASRs, would be weakly supported. High QWK and a tiny ΔASR could come almost entirely from agreement on refusals and low scores. Agreement at the 3-versus-4 boundary, which decides success, would be largely untested.
rubric: Identifies reliable ASR or success classification at the s≥4 threshold as weakly supported
Explains that the agreement could be driven by easy low-score or refusal cases, leaving the 3-versus-4 decision boundary untested

items.question: If the human-expert validation of GPT-5 had used responses from the 8 proprietary models only, which reported results would have the weakest judge support?
items.answer: The GPT-5-scored results for the 8 open-weight models would have the weakest support, along with any open-weight-versus-proprietary comparison. Their responses could differ in style, for example in how often they misread or give irrelevant replies. Agreement measured on proprietary responses would not directly cover them.
rubric: Names the open-weight models' scores, or open-vs-proprietary comparisons, as weakest
Explains that validation on proprietary responses does not cover the possibly different response styles of open-weight models

items.question: Does the paper show that the visual inputs across its 272 intents are diverse and non-redundant? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The diversity analysis embeds only the intent text, using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with PCA and pairwise similarity. The generated images were filtered for relevance, quality and readability, but their diversity across intents was never measured.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the similarity and PCA analyses cover the text intents only, and no diversity analysis of the images is reported

items.question: Does the paper show that scenario-level estimates for Sexual Content are less precise than those for other scenarios? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted, as far as intent counts go. Sexual Content is small only at the domain level, where it has 17 intents against 28–48 for other domains. Its single scenario has 17 intents, as many as or more than every other scenario, which range from 14 to 17. Its scenario-level interval should therefore be no wider than the others.
rubric: Answers contradicted (precision is not lower at scenario level), or equivalent
Explains that its single scenario has 17 intents, at least as many as other scenarios (14–17), and that the small-stratum caution applies at the domain level

items.question: Does the paper show that a model's MMJailBench ASR predicts its vulnerability on other multimodal jailbreak benchmarks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. No cross-benchmark correlation is reported. The paper stresses that ASR depends on the specific mixture of intents, framings, images and carriers, and that comparisons are valid only under the same judge, rubric and benchmark version.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites that no cross-benchmark analysis is given, and that ASR depends on the benchmark mixture and on judge or rubric choices

items.question: Does the paper show that the lightweight configuration reproduces full-configuration results for individual harmful intents? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Stratification covers domains, framings, visual conditions and carriers, not individual intents. With 1,500 instances spread over 272 intents, each intent gets only about 5–6 instances. Agreement is shown only over 32 matched cells.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that sampling is stratified by domain, framing, visual condition and carrier rather than by intent, leaving few instances per intent, and that agreement is reported only over 32 cells

items.question: Does the paper show that its cross-modal attention tooling identifies which parts of an image, such as the text on an authorization document, the model attends to? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The tooling sums attention over the group of visual tokens per layer and averages over heads. It gives one visual-attention profile per condition, with no breakdown by image region. Attention is also described as an imperfect indicator of information flow.
rubric: Answers not settled (or not supported)
Explains that attention is aggregated over all visual tokens per layer and averaged over heads, giving no region-level breakdown

items.question: Does the paper's description imply that each of the 6 framing templates has roughly the same share, about 250 instances, in the lightweight configuration? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Supported. The lightweight configuration is stratified over framings and preserves the full-configuration distribution. In the full configuration every intent is crossed with every template, so each template holds an equal one-sixth share, about 250 of 1,500 instances.
rubric: Answers supported
Explains that stratified sampling preserves the full-configuration distribution, in which each template has an equal one-sixth share (about 250 instances)

items.question: Would comparing ASR between the Danger and Role categories be free of differences caused by the image generator used?
items.answer: Yes. Both Danger and Role images were generated with zimage, so the generator is held constant. Other differences, such as category content and filtering, remain.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that both categories were generated with the same model (zimage)

items.question: Would comparing ASR between the Danger and Authorization Document categories be free of differences caused by the image generator used?
items.answer: No. Danger images come from zimage, while Authorization Document images come from a 4-bit-quantized FLUX.2, chosen for coherent text. Generator differences in quality and legibility are confounded with category.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that Danger uses zimage while Authorization Document uses FLUX.2

items.question: Does GPT-5's reported ΔASR of +0.3% against human experts directly validate ASR computed at the paper's default threshold s≥4?
items.answer: Yes. ASR is defined at s≥4, so a ΔASR of +0.3% directly shows that GPT-5 and the experts yield nearly the same success rate at that threshold.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that ΔASR compares ASR, which is defined at the s≥4 threshold

items.question: Does GPT-5's reported ΔASR of +0.3% against human experts directly validate an ASR that a user recomputes at threshold s≥3 from the released scores?
items.answer: No. ΔASR was measured for the default s≥4 definition. QWK of 0.97 indicates broad ordinal agreement but does not directly bound the rate gap at s≥3, so the user should re-validate at the new threshold.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that ΔASR refers to the s≥4 definition, and QWK alone does not directly validate rates at another threshold (re-validation needed)

items.question: For TEXT-carrier instances, can the cross-modal attention tooling measure attention from the final prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens in the instruction?
items.answer: Yes. Under TEXT the harmful instruction is in the textual input, so its harm-related label tokens exist as text tokens that the tooling can target.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that the instruction, and hence the harm-related label tokens, are present as text tokens

items.question: For OCR-carrier instances, can the cross-modal attention tooling measure attention from the final prefix query to harm-related task-label tokens in the instruction?
items.answer: No, not as defined. Under OCR the instruction is rendered into the image, so the harm-related words reach the model as visual tokens rather than as textual label tokens. Only the overall visual-token attention would be measured.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that the instruction is rendered into the image, so there are no textual harm-label tokens to target

items.question: Is the lightweight configuration guaranteed by its described construction to include instances from the Sexual Content domain?
items.answer: Yes. It is stratified over harm domains while preserving the full distribution, so Sexual Content gets roughly 6.3% of 1,500, about 94 instances.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that sampling is stratified by harm domain, preserving its roughly 6.3% share

items.question: Is the lightweight configuration guaranteed by its described construction to include every one of the 272 individual intents?
items.answer: No. Stratification is over domains, framings, visual conditions and carriers, not over individual intents, so the described procedure does not guarantee every intent appears.
rubric: Answers no (not guaranteed)
Explains that intents are not a stratification variable; only domains, framings, visual conditions and carriers are

items.question: Can a difference direction fitted on gemma3-12b discovery pairs be used to project held-out gemma3-12b pairs?
items.answer: Yes. This is the tooling's intended check: the direction is fitted and tested in the same model's residual-stream space, on new samples.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that discovery and held-out activations come from the same model's residual stream

items.question: Can a difference direction fitted on gemma3-12b discovery pairs be used to project held-out qwen3-vl-8b pairs?
items.answer: No. The direction is defined in gemma3-12b's residual-stream space, and qwen3-vl-8b has its own internal representation space. The direction must be refitted on qwen3-vl-8b's own discovery pairs.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that the direction lives in one model's residual-stream space and must be refitted for another model

items.question: When would comparing a model's OCR CASR with its TEXT CASR fail to isolate the effect of the delivery channel, even if the judge's mismatch flags are perfectly accurate?
items.answer: The comparison fails when OCR mismatches are concentrated in particular intents, templates or domains rather than spread at random. CASR drops mismatched responses from its denominator, so OCR CASR would then be computed over a different mixture of intents and framings than TEXT CASR. Because ASR-type rates depend on that mixture, part of the CASR gap would reflect composition rather than the carrier.
rubric: States the comparison fails when mismatches are non-randomly concentrated, for example in certain intents, templates or domains.
Explains that excluding mismatched cases leaves OCR CASR computed over a different intent or framing mixture than TEXT, and rates depend on that mixture, so the gap is partly compositional.

items.question: A user requests a per-intent cross-tabulation and reads the suite's bootstrap confidence interval for one individual harmful intent. Why would that interval fail to describe the uncertainty of that intent's ASR?
items.answer: The suite resamples intents, and a stratum containing a single intent always resamples that same intent. The interval therefore collapses to a point or near-zero width. It ignores the variation among that intent's responses across framings, images and carriers, so it understates the uncertainty.
rubric: States that the interval collapses or becomes degenerate (near-zero width) and understates uncertainty.
Explains that resampling intents within a one-intent stratum always returns the same intent, so variation across that intent's responses is not captured.

items.question: When would the pooled Story row of a model's prompt-framing table misrepresent how Story framing works on that model under the TEXT carrier specifically?
items.answer: The Story row averages over both carriers and all visual conditions. If Story framing interacts with the carrier, for example raising ASR strongly only under OCR, the pooled rate would mix the two and misstate Story's effect under TEXT. A framing-by-carrier cross-tabulation is needed to see this.
rubric: States the pooled row misleads when framing interacts with carrier (or another dimension), i.e. Story's effect differs by carrier.
Explains that the framing table is a marginal averaged over carriers and visual conditions, so a cross-tabulation is needed.

items.question: An auditor uses the per-model factor-sensitivity scatter plot to decide which models deserve closer inspection. When would a model with a very large ASR range go unflagged by this plot?
items.answer: The plot encodes only three dimensions: two axes and marker size. There are four annotated dimensions, so one is always left out. A model whose large range lies on the omitted dimension would look unremarkable, and a second plot or the range table is needed.
rubric: States the model is missed when its large range is on the dimension not shown in the plot.
Explains that the plot shows only three of the four annotated dimensions (two axes plus marker size).

items.question: When would the paper's near-duplicate filtering of harmful intents fail to remove two intents that pursue essentially the same harmful objective?
items.answer: Filtering inspects only the high-similarity tail of all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine similarities. Two intents that describe the same objective with very different wording could get a low embedding similarity. They would then fall outside the manually reviewed tail and both remain.
rubric: States filtering fails for same-objective intents phrased with different wording that receive low embedding similarity.
Explains that only the high-similarity tail was manually reviewed, so low-similarity pairs are never inspected.

items.question: For which kind of model would OCR CASR computed on the 1,500-instance lightweight configuration be too imprecise to support conclusions, and why?
items.answer: It would be too imprecise for a model with a very high OCR mismatch rate. The lightweight configuration gives each model only about 750 OCR instances, and CASR's denominator excludes mismatches. At 80% mismatch, for instance, only around 150 responses remain, and far fewer per stratum, so the intervals become wide.
rubric: Identifies models with a high OCR mismatch rate.
Explains that the CASR denominator excludes mismatches, and the lightweight configuration already has only about 750 OCR instances per model, so few responses remain.

items.question: Suppose GPT-5 systematically over-scores Code-framed responses relative to human experts. Would the lightweight judge's reported validation reveal this problem, and why?
items.answer: No. The lightweight judge was trained on GPT-5 annotations and validated only against GPT-5, so it would likely inherit the same bias and still show high agreement. Only comparison with human labels could expose the bias, and the paper reports only pooled GPT-5-versus-human agreement, not agreement per framing.
rubric: States the validation would not reveal the bias, and the lightweight judge would likely share it.
Explains that the judge was trained on and validated against GPT-5 labels, so a bias they share is invisible to that agreement check.

items.question: On an OCR instance, a model misreads the embedded instruction and produces detailed operational guidance for a different harmful task. Why might neither ASR nor CASR register this harmful output?
items.answer: ASR counts substantive assistance to the targeted harmful intent. Misinterpreting the evaluated intent is classed as a mismatch, so the response is dropped from the CASR denominator and does not count as a success for the target intent. A harmful but off-target answer can therefore escape both metrics.
rubric: States the output may not be counted as a success in either metric.
Explains that success is defined relative to the targeted intent, while misinterpretation is flagged as a mismatch and removed from the CASR denominator.

items.question: For a new model, when could the lightweight configuration's ASR deviate from the full configuration by more than the maximum difference reported in Table 11?
items.answer: This could happen when the model's successful jailbreaks are concentrated in a few intents or instances. Whether those few cases are sampled into the 1,500 instances then dominates the estimate. Table 11's differences were measured on the evaluated models, so they do not bound sampling error for a model with such skewed vulnerability.
rubric: States large deviation can occur when the model's successes are concentrated in a few intents or instances.
Explains that the estimate then depends heavily on whether those cases are sampled, and Table 11's bounds come only from the evaluated models.

items.question: Why would intent-resampled bootstrap confidence intervals for a model's aggregate ASR tend to be wider on the lightweight configuration than on the full configuration?
items.answer: On the lightweight configuration, each intent contributes only about 1,500/272 ≈ 5–6 responses per model, compared with dozens in the full configuration. Each intent's success rate is therefore estimated much more noisily, and some intents may be absent. Resampling these noisier intent-level values gives wider intervals.
rubric: States the intervals are wider because each intent has far fewer responses (about 5–6 per model versus dozens).
Explains that noisier intent-level estimates (and possibly missing intents) increase the variability captured by resampling intents.

items.question: Why can Table 11's 95% CI for the mean lightweight-minus-full ASR difference be as narrow as [-0.45%, 0.30%] when individual matched cells differ by up to 3.53%?
items.answer: The interval describes the mean difference over 32 cells, not any single cell. Cell-level deviations of both signs largely cancel when averaged, so the mean is estimated precisely even though individual cells vary by several points.
rubric: States the CI concerns the mean across the 32 cells, not individual cells.
Explains that averaging cancels positive and negative cell deviations, so the mean is precise despite large individual differences.

items.question: Taking ΔASR as GPT-5's ASR minus the human experts' ASR, why does Table 12 suggest that any bias in GPT-5-scored ASRs would lean toward overstating rather than understating model vulnerability, and by how much?
items.answer: GPT-5 counts slightly more responses as successes (score ≥4) than humans do, with ΔASR = +0.3%. Any bias therefore leans toward reporting more jailbreaks than experts would. The size is only about 0.3 percentage points, which is negligible for most comparisons.
rubric: States the bias leans toward overstating vulnerability, because GPT-5 marks slightly more successes than humans.
Gives the magnitude as about 0.3 percentage points, i.e. negligible.

items.question: The paper warns that a large per-model range along a dimension may come from a single outlying configuration or from a gradual trend. Why does this distinction carry no information for the instruction-carrier dimension?
items.answer: The carrier dimension has only two configurations, TEXT and OCR. Its range is simply the absolute difference between the two ASRs. With two points there is no way to separate an outlier from a trend, so the range already says everything.
rubric: States the distinction is meaningless or uninformative for the carrier dimension.
Explains that with only two carriers the range equals |TEXT − OCR|, so an outlier cannot be distinguished from a trend.

items.question: Why might the suite be unable to report a CASR value for a stratum in which a model fails to interpret every OCR instruction?
items.answer: CASR = N_success / (N − N_mismatch). If every response in the stratum is a mismatch, the denominator is zero, so CASR is undefined. ASR can still be computed and would be near zero.
rubric: States CASR would be undefined or unavailable.
Explains that the denominator N − N_mismatch becomes zero when all responses are mismatches.

items.question: A model has identical ASR on TEXT and OCR inputs. Why is its OCR mismatch rate still needed before concluding that the carrier makes no difference to its safety?
items.answer: If many OCR inputs are mismatched, the same number of successes is spread over fewer understood inputs. OCR CASR would then exceed TEXT CASR. Equal ASRs can therefore hide the fact that, when the model does read the embedded instruction, it complies more often than under TEXT.
rubric: States that equal ASRs can hide a carrier difference, because OCR CASR may be higher than TEXT CASR.
Explains that OCR mismatches shrink the CASR denominator, so successes among understood OCR inputs form a larger share.

items.question: Under Eq. 1, for a fixed harmful intent, framing template and TEXT carrier, is the instruction text identical across the five visual semantic categories?
items.answer: Yes. The instruction component L(h,t,c) does not depend on the visual condition v. Only the image V(h,v) changes across visual categories.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that L(h,t,c) has no dependence on v; only V(h,v) varies.

items.question: Under Eq. 1, for a fixed harmful intent, visual semantic category and TEXT carrier, is the instruction text identical across the six framing templates?
items.answer: No. The framing t is an argument of L(h,t,c), so the instruction text changes with the template, while the image V(h,v) stays the same.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that framing t enters L(h,t,c), so the instruction text differs across templates.

items.question: Following the paper's advice to aggregate to the domain level when confidence intervals become wide, would aggregating the Sexual Content scenario to its domain narrow its confidence interval?
items.answer: No. The Sexual Content domain contains a single scenario. Its domain-level stratum holds the same 17 intents as the scenario, so aggregating changes nothing.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that Sexual Content has only one scenario, so the domain and scenario contain the same 17 intents.

items.question: Following the paper's advice to aggregate to the domain level when confidence intervals become wide, would aggregating the Suicide & Self-Harm scenario to its domain narrow its confidence interval?
items.answer: Yes. The scenario has 15 intents, while its domain, Violence & Physical Harm, has 48 across three scenarios. Resampling over more intents gives a narrower interval, though the estimate then no longer refers to self-harm alone.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the domain has 48 intents versus 15 in the scenario, so resampling more intents narrows the interval.

items.question: If an auditor adds the four control image conditions to the five semantic categories when computing a model's ASR range on the visual dimension, could that range become smaller?
items.answer: No. A range is the maximum minus the minimum over the configurations. Adding configurations to the set can never lower the maximum or raise the minimum.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the range over a superset of configurations cannot be smaller, since the max cannot drop and the min cannot rise.

items.question: If an auditor adds the four control image conditions to the five semantic categories when computing a model's ASR range on the visual dimension, could that range become larger?
items.answer: Yes. If any control condition yields an ASR above the highest or below the lowest semantic category, the range widens. Ranges are therefore comparable only when computed over the same set of configurations.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the range widens whenever a control's ASR falls outside the semantic categories' min–max.

items.question: Is it consistent with Table 11 that the lightweight configuration overestimates ASR in every one of the 32 matched cells?
items.answer: No. If every cell had a positive lightweight-minus-full difference, the mean difference would be positive. Table 11 reports a mean of −0.06%.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that all-positive differences would give a positive mean, contradicting the reported −0.06%.

items.question: Is it consistent with Table 11 that the lightweight configuration overestimates ASR in at least one of the 32 matched cells?
items.answer: Yes, and in fact Table 11 requires it. The mean absolute difference (0.79%) far exceeds the magnitude of the mean difference (0.06%). That is only possible if the differences have both signs, so some cells must be positive.
rubric: Answers yes, and notes that it must be so.
Explains that a mean absolute difference much larger than |mean difference| implies differences of both signs.

items.question: Would a 5-percentage-point lightweight-versus-full ASR difference in a single matched cell lie outside the range of cell differences reported in Table 11?
items.answer: Yes. Table 11's maximum absolute cell difference is 3.53%, so a 5-point gap exceeds anything reported.
rubric: Answers yes.
Cites the maximum absolute difference of 3.53% as below 5 points.

items.question: Would a 3-percentage-point lightweight-versus-full ASR difference in a single matched cell lie outside the range of cell differences reported in Table 11?
items.answer: No. Two of the 32 cells exceed 2%, and the maximum is 3.53%, so a 3-point gap falls within the reported range, although it is unusually large.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the maximum is 3.53% and two cells exceed 2%, so 3 points is within the reported range.

items.question: A researcher wants to use the representation-level tooling on qwen3-vl-8b to study how TEXT versus OCR delivery changes internal states. How should the matched pairs be built, and what should be done about OCR perception failures?
items.answer: Each pair should share the harmful intent, framing template and visual semantic category, and differ only in carrier. Pairs whose OCR response is flagged as a mismatch should be excluded or analyzed separately, so that perception failures do not drive the divergence. Even then, the carrier change alters both the text tokens and the image content, and the result remains correlational.
rubric: States pairs must hold intent, framing and visual category fixed while varying only the carrier.
Recommends excluding or separating OCR cases flagged as mismatches, so perception failures do not drive the result.
Notes that the carrier change alters both the text and the image (or that the result is correlational).

items.question: An auditor wants to compare harm categories using strata of roughly equal size, so that differences in precision do not drive the comparison. Should they use the domain level or the scenario level of the harmful-intent stratification, and why?
items.answer: They should use the scenario level. The 18 scenarios each contain 14–17 intents, whereas domains range from 17 (Sexual Content) to 48 (Violence & Physical Harm). Scenario-level strata are therefore much more uniform in size.
rubric: Chooses the scenario level.
Explains that scenarios have 14–17 intents each, while domains range from 17 to 48.

items.question: A team scored its old model release with GPT-5 (12.4% ASR) and its new release with the lightweight judge (12.0% ASR). Can it claim the new release is safer, and what should it do?
items.answer: No. The 0.4-point drop equals the lightweight judge's reported ΔASR of −0.4% relative to GPT-5, so it could be entirely a judge offset. Both releases should be scored with the same judge, under the same decoding settings and benchmark version.
rubric: States the claim is not supported.
Explains that the drop matches the lightweight judge's −0.4% ΔASR relative to GPT-5, so the judge alone could explain it.
Recommends rescoring both releases with the same judge.

items.question: A researcher wants to test whether a model's refusals are sensitive to low-level visual statistics of an image when the image carries no semantic content. Which two released control conditions should be compared, and why?
items.answer: The blank and random-noise images should be compared. Both carry no semantic content and share the same resolution and instruction, but they differ in low-level visual statistics. Any ASR difference between them would point to sensitivity to pixel-level content or preprocessing rather than meaning, which should be checked as the paper recommends.
rubric: Names the blank and noise controls.
Explains that both lack semantic content and share instructions and resolution, so a difference reflects low-level visual statistics or preprocessing rather than meaning.

items.question: A group adds 50 new harmful intents to MMJailBench. Following the paper's construction procedure, how should it check for redundancy, and what must it note when reporting aggregate ASR?
items.answer: It should compute all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine similarities among the new intents and against the existing 272, then manually review the high-similarity tail to remove near-duplicates. The extended set is a different benchmark version and changes the intent mixture. Its aggregate ASR is therefore not directly comparable with results on the original version.
rubric: Describes embedding-based pairwise similarity (including against existing intents) with manual review of the high-similarity tail.
Notes that aggregates are not comparable with the original version, because the benchmark version and intent mixture changed.

items.question: A team wants to evaluate a text-only LLM on MMJailBench and compare it with the paper's MLLMs. Which part of the benchmark can it use, and what is the valid comparison?
items.answer: It can use only TEXT-carrier instances under the no-image control, since OCR and the semantic or control images all require visual input. The valid comparison is against the MLLMs' results on that same TEXT/no-image stratum. Comparing with their aggregate ASR would be invalid, because aggregate ASR depends on a different mixture of conditions.
rubric: States that only TEXT-carrier instances with the no-image control are usable.
States the comparison must be with MLLM results on the same stratum, not their aggregate ASR, because aggregates depend on the mixture of conditions.

items.question: After finding that gemma3-12b's representations diverge most between authority-document and danger images at certain layers, a team wants to test whether that difference drives the model's compliance. What must it add to the paper's tooling?
items.answer: It must add an intervention. For example, it could add or subtract the fitted difference direction in the residual stream at the most-divergent layers, then measure whether judged ASR changes. The divergence profile and held-out projection alone are correlational and cannot show causation.
rubric: States an intervention is required, such as steering or ablating along the difference direction and measuring the behavioral change.
Explains that the tooling's divergence and projection results are only correlational.

items.question: If the control images had been paired with different instruction components from the semantic images, which use of the controls would lose its support?
items.answer: Comparing semantic categories against control conditions to isolate the role of image content would lose support. Any ASR difference would then be confounded with differences in the instruction text, which under Eq. 1 is meant to be held fixed when only the visual input changes.
rubric: Identifies the semantic-versus-control comparison of image content.
Explains that differing instructions would confound the comparison, since only the image should vary.

items.question: If the Paradox template had turned harmful requests into genuinely different, safety-oriented questions instead of preserving the underlying intent, which result would be undermined, and how?
items.answer: The Paradox row of the framing stratification would be undermined. Its ASR would mix the framing effect with a changed objective. Because success and mismatch are judged against the targeted intent, many Paradox responses could be scored as off-target or mismatched, so the ASR difference from other templates would no longer reflect framing alone.
rubric: Identifies the per-framing (Paradox) ASR and its comparison with other templates.
Explains that a changed intent confounds framing with objective, since success and mismatch are judged against the targeted intent.

items.question: If generated images had not been filtered for semantic relevance, which stratification's interpretation would lose support, and why?
items.answer: The visual-semantics stratification would lose support. Category labels such as Authorization Document or Role would no longer reliably indicate that the image conveys that contextual signal. Per-category ASR differences could then reflect off-category or irrelevant images rather than the intended semantics.
rubric: Identifies the visual-semantics stratification.
Explains that without relevance filtering, images may not convey their labeled category, so category ASRs may not reflect the intended semantics.

items.question: If OCR instances existed for only a subset of intents while TEXT instances existed for all 272, which comparison would be confounded, and why?
items.answer: The TEXT-versus-OCR carrier comparison would be confounded. The two carriers would pool different intent mixtures, and since ASR depends on the mixture of intents, part of any carrier difference would reflect composition rather than delivery.
rubric: Identifies the TEXT-versus-OCR carrier comparison.
Explains that the carriers would cover different intent mixtures, and ASR depends on the mixture.

items.question: If the 1,500-instance configuration had been sampled with equal numbers of instances per harm domain instead of preserving the full configuration's distribution, which Table 11 result would most likely worsen, and why?
items.answer: The near-zero mean ASR difference, and with it the concordance, would likely worsen. Violence & Physical Harm (17.6% of intents) would be underweighted and Sexual Content (6.3%) overweighted relative to the full configuration. If domains differ in ASR, the lightweight aggregate would shift systematically.
rubric: Identifies the mean ASR difference or concordance (agreement in level) as likely to worsen.
Explains that equal allocation reweights domains (for example, Violence underweighted and Sexual Content overweighted), biasing the aggregate when domain ASRs differ.

items.question: Does the paper show that all 16 models were run with identical sampling parameters? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Sampling parameters were fixed only where provider interfaces permit. For interfaces that do not expose them, default settings were used and documented. Cross-model comparisons involving such models therefore carry a decoding caveat.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Explains that some proprietary interfaces did not expose sampling parameters, so defaults were used for those models.

items.question: Does the paper show that MMJailBench's harmful intents are novel relative to existing safety benchmarks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The taxonomy was built from existing safety benchmarks, including multimodal ones, and from provider policies. Intents were then normalized and filtered. The diversity claim concerns redundancy within the set, not novelty relative to prior benchmarks.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Explains that the intents were derived from existing benchmarks and provider policies, and that the diversity analysis concerns only redundancy within the set.

items.question: Does the paper show that the lightweight judge reproduces GPT-5's ASR for each of the 16 evaluated models individually? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Table 12 reports only pooled agreement (QWK 0.95, ΔASR −0.4%). Per-model differences could be larger and of varying sign, and no per-model agreement is reported.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that only pooled agreement statistics are reported, with no per-model breakdown.

items.question: Does the paper show, with reported statistics, that each generated image depicts its intended visual semantic category? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Images are said to be filtered for semantic relevance, visual quality and readability through predefined procedures. However, the paper reports no category-verification statistics or annotator agreement for images.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that filtering is described but no image-level verification results or agreement statistics are reported.

items.question: Does the paper show that the 18 harm scenarios contain roughly equal numbers of intents? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Supported. Table 5 lists every scenario with 14 to 17 intents, about 5.1–6.3% each. This contrasts with the much more uneven domain sizes, which run from 17 to 48.
rubric: Answers supported.
Cites scenario sizes of about 14–17 intents (5.1–6.3%) from Table 5.

rejected.question: Suppose Table 11 had kept Spearman 0.997 but reported a 95% CI for the mean ASR difference of [0.5%, 1.2%]. Which use of the lightweight configuration would lose support, and which would remain?
rejected.answer: Directly comparing lightweight ASR numbers with full-configuration ASR numbers would lose support, because the CI would exclude zero and indicate a systematic upward offset. Ranking models or cells with the lightweight configuration would still be supported, because rank agreement stays high.
rubric: States that direct comparison of absolute ASR values between lightweight and full results would lose support, because of a systematic offset (CI excludes zero)
States that rank-based uses such as ordering models would remain supported by the high Spearman
